## 3. Weak Hardness for Stable Algorithms

In this section, we will show that under certain conditions, stable quantum algorithms fail to find near-optimal solutions for the Quantum Hypergraph Max-Cut problem in the average case. We call this a weak hardness result because the locality $k$ at which the problem becomes hard is dependent on the Lipschitz constant $L$ of the algorithm—thus, this result cannot be used to prove that there exists a single $k$ for which the problem is hard for all stable algorithms. The proofs in this section are largely adapted from Anschuetz (2026), but significantly simplified.

#### Definition 3.1 (Quantum algorithm).

A quantum algorithm is described by a map $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}:\mathbb{R}^{D}\times\Omega\rightarrow\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{m}}_{n}$ , where $\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{m}}_{n}$ is the set of mixed states on $n$ qubits, $(\Omega,\mathbb{P})$ is a probability space, and in our case, $D=\binom{n}{k}$ . We say that the algorithm is deterministic if the probability space $(\Omega,\mathbb{P})$ is trivial, and it is pure if it has codomain $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ (the set of pure quantum states).

#### Definition 3.2 (Associated pure quantum algorithm).

Since we can view mixed states as probability distributions over pure states, for any deterministic quantum algorithm $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}$ , there is an associated pure quantum algorithm $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}$ such that

$$ \boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X})=\EE_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right]. $$

#### Definition 3.3 (Stable quantum algorithm).

Let $\Xi$ be a probability distribution over pairs $(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime})$ of problem instances that correspond to the same interaction hypergraph (i.e. $X_{A}=0\iff X^{\prime}_{A}=0$ ). Then, we say that a quantum algorithm $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}$ is $(f,L,\mathfrak{d},\Xi,p_{\mathrm{st}})$ -stable if we have that

$$ \Pr_{(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\sim\Xi\otimes\mathbb{P}_{\Omega}}\left[\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)-\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rVert_{W_{2}}\leq f+L\left\lVert\boldsymbol{X}-\boldsymbol{X}\right\rVert_{1}\mid\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}\left(\boldsymbol{X}\right)\right]\geq 1-p_{\mathrm{st}}, $$

where $\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}\left(\boldsymbol{X}\right)$ is the event that the interaction hypergraph of $\boldsymbol{X}$ has degree at most $\mathfrak{d}$ , i.e. for all $v\in[n]$ , we have that

$$ \left\lvert\left\{A\in\binom{[n]}{k}:v\in A\wedge X_{A}\neq 0\right\}\right\rvert\leq\mathfrak{d}. $$

#### Definition 3.4 (Near-optimal quantum algorithm).

A quantum algorithm is $(\gamma,p_{\mathrm{f}})$ -optimal for a distribution $\Lambda$ of problem instances if

$$ \Pr_{(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\sim\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{P}_{\Omega}}\left[\Tr\left(\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right)\geq\gamma E_{\ast}\right]\geq 1-p_{\mathrm{f}}. $$

### 3.1. Stable Algorithms Imply the Existence of Forbidden Configurations

#### 3.1.1. Reduction to Weakly Stable Algorithms with Classical Outputs

In the following lemmas, we will first perform a reduction where we convert a stable randomized quantum algorithm into a deterministic one, and then we will apply the classical shadows estimator to convert it into an algorithm outputting classical states that satisfies a weaker version of the stability condition.

#### Lemma 3.5.

(From Anschuetz (2026, Lemma 27)) Let $\Xi$ be a probability distribution of pairs of problem instances on the same hypergraph, whose marginal distributions are both $\Lambda$ . Suppose that there exists a quantum algorithm $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)$ that is $\left(f,L,\mathfrak{d},\Xi,p_{\mathrm{st}}\right)$ -stable and $(\gamma,p_{\mathrm{f}})$ -optimal for $\Lambda$ . Then, there exists a deterministic quantum algorithm $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}(\boldsymbol{X})$ that is $\left(f,L,\mathfrak{d},\Xi,3p_{\mathrm{st}}\right)$ -stable and $(\gamma,3p_{\mathrm{f}})$ -optimal for $\Lambda$ .

#### Proof.

We have that

$$ \displaystyle\EE_{\omega\sim\mathbb{P}_{\Omega}}\left[\Pr_{(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime})\sim\Xi}\left[\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)-\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rVert_{W_{2}}>f+L\left\lVert\boldsymbol{X}-\boldsymbol{X}\right\rVert_{1}\mid\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}(\boldsymbol{X})\right]\right]= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\Pr_{(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\sim\Xi\otimes\mathbb{P}_{\Omega}}\left[\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)-\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rVert_{W_{2}}>f+L\left\lVert\boldsymbol{X}-\boldsymbol{X}\right\rVert_{1}\mid\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}(\boldsymbol{X})\right]\leq p_{\mathrm{st}}, $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\EE_{\omega\sim\mathbb{P}_{\Omega}}\left[\Pr_{\boldsymbol{X}\sim\Lambda}\left[\Tr\left(\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right)<\gamma E_{\ast}\right]\right]= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\Pr_{(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\sim\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{P}_{\Omega}}\left[\Tr\left(\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right)<\gamma E_{\ast}\right]\leq p_{\mathrm{f}}. $$

So, by Markov’s inequality, we have that

$$ \displaystyle\Pr_{\omega\sim\mathbb{P}_{\Omega}}\Bigg[\Pr_{(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime})\sim\Xi}\Big[\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)-\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rVert_{W_{2}}> \displaystyle>f+L\left\lVert\boldsymbol{X}-\boldsymbol{X}\right\rVert_{1}\mid\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}(\boldsymbol{X})\Big]>3p_{\mathrm{st}}\Bigg]\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\frac{1}{3p_{\mathrm{st}}}\EE_{\omega\sim\mathbb{P}_{\Omega}}\Bigg[\Pr_{(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime})\sim\Xi}\Big[\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)-\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rVert_{W_{2}}> \displaystyle>f+L\left\lVert\boldsymbol{X}-\boldsymbol{X}\right\rVert_{1}\mid\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}(\boldsymbol{X})\Big]\Bigg]\leq\frac{1}{3}, $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\Pr_{\omega\sim\mathbb{P}_{\Omega}}\left[\Pr_{\boldsymbol{X}\sim\Lambda}\left[\Tr\left(\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right)<\gamma E_{\ast}\right]>3p_{\mathrm{f}}\right]\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\frac{1}{3p_{\mathrm{f}}}\EE_{\omega\sim\mathbb{P}_{\Omega}}\left[\Pr_{\boldsymbol{X}\sim\Lambda}\left[\Tr\left(\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right)<\gamma E_{\ast}\right]\right]\leq\frac{1}{3}. $$

So now, by the union bound, we have that

$$ \displaystyle\Pr_{\omega\sim\mathbb{P}_{\Omega}}\Bigg[\Pr_{\boldsymbol{X}\sim\Lambda}\left[\Tr\left(\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right)<\gamma E_{\ast}\right]>3p_{\mathrm{f}}\vee \displaystyle\vee\Pr_{(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime})\sim\Xi}\left[\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)-\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rVert_{W_{2}}>f+L\left\lVert\boldsymbol{X}-\boldsymbol{X}\right\rVert_{1}\right]>3p_{\mathrm{st}}\mid\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}(\boldsymbol{X})\Bigg]\leq\frac{2}{3}. $$

Thus, there must exist some $\omega^{\ast}\in\Omega$ such that we have

$$ \Pr_{(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime})\sim\Xi}\left[\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega^{\ast})-\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega^{\ast})\right\rVert_{W_{2}}\leq f+L\left\lVert\boldsymbol{X}-\boldsymbol{X}\right\rVert_{1}\mid\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}(\boldsymbol{X})\right]\geq 1-3p_{\mathrm{st}}, $$

and

$$ \Pr_{\boldsymbol{X}\sim\Lambda}\left[\Tr\left(\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega^{\ast})\right)\geq\gamma E_{\ast}\right]\geq 1-3p_{\mathrm{f}}. $$

Thus, if we define $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}(\boldsymbol{X})\coloneq\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega^{\ast})$ , then $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}$ is a deterministic quantum algorithm that is $\left(f,L,\Xi,3p_{\mathrm{st}}\right)$ -stable and $(\gamma,3p_{\mathrm{f}})$ -optimal. ∎

Now, if we have a stable and near-optimal deterministic quantum algorithm, we can apply the shadows estimator to it, obtaining a randomized algorithm that only outputs classical states. This algorithm will be close to $1/3$ -optimal with high probability and it will stable in expectation (which is a weaker notion than stability as we have previously defined it).

#### Lemma 3.6.

(Modified version of Anschuetz (2026, Lemma 28)) Let $\Xi$ be a probability distribution of pairs of problem instances on the same hypergraph whose marginal distributions are both $\Lambda$ . Suppose that the Pauli shadows estimator is $(\delta,p_{\mathrm{est}},p_{\mathrm{b}})$ -efficient for the class of Hamiltonians $\boldsymbol{H}(\Lambda)$ . Suppose there exists a deterministic quantum algorithm $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}$ that is $\left(f,L,\mathfrak{d},\Xi,3p_{\mathrm{st}}\right)$ -stable and $(\gamma,3p_{\mathrm{f}})$ -optimal for $\Lambda$ . Then, there exists a pure quantum algorithm $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}:\mathbb{R}^{\binom{n}{k}}\times[0,1]\rightarrow\{0,1\}^{n}$ (that is, a randomized algorithm outputting only classical states), such that the following weaker notion of stability holds:

$$ \displaystyle\Pr_{(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime})\sim\Xi}\Bigg[\left\lVert\EE_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right|-\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right|\right]\right\rVert_{W_{2}}\leq \displaystyle\leq{}f+L\left\lVert\boldsymbol{X}-\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{1}\mid\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}(\boldsymbol{X})\Bigg]\geq 1-3p_{\mathrm{st}}. $$

Furthermore, consider some $\boldsymbol{X}$ that satisfies the following two conditions (which is true with probability at least $1-3p_{\mathrm{f}}-p_{\mathrm{b}}$ over $\boldsymbol{X}\sim\Lambda$ ):

$$ \Tr\left(\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}(\boldsymbol{X})\right)\geq\gamma E_{\ast} $$

$$ \Pr_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[\Tr\left(3\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{M}}}(\boldsymbol{\rho},\omega)\right)-\Tr\left(\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\boldsymbol{\rho}\right)\geq-\delta E_{\ast}\right]\geq 1-p_{\mathrm{est}}\quad\forall\boldsymbol{\rho}\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{m}}_{n}. $$

For such $\boldsymbol{X}$ , we must have that

$$ \Pr_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[V\left(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right)\geq\frac{1}{3}(\gamma-\delta)E_{\ast}\right]\geq 1-p_{\mathrm{est}}. $$

#### Proof.

We define $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)$ as follows. First, run the deterministic quantum algorithm $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X})$ to obtain a quantum state $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ . Then randomly choose one of the $X$ , $Y$ , and $Z$ bases and measure $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ in that basis, outputting the resulting bit string. Consider the related algorithm $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}^{\prime}$ defined as

$$ \boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\coloneq\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{M}}}(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}(\boldsymbol{X}),\omega). $$

That is, if the result of measuring the qubits in basis $b$ was the bit string $\mathbf{s}$ , the output of $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}$ is $\mathbf{s}$ while the output of $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}^{\prime}}$ is $\left|b;\mathbf{s}\right\rangle$ . Observe that since our model is symmetric with respect to exchanging $X$ , $Y$ , and $Z$ bases, we have that

$$ \left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right|\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right\rangle=\Tr\left(\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right). $$

Now, we have the following:

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert\EE_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right|-\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right|\right]\right\rVert_{W_{2}}\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\left\lVert\EE_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right]-\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rVert_{W_{2}}= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\left\lVert\EE_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{M}}}(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}(\boldsymbol{X}),\omega)-\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{M}}}(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime}),\omega)\right]\right\rVert_{W_{2}}= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\mathcal{M}}(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}(\boldsymbol{X}))-\boldsymbol{\mathcal{M}}(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime}))\right\rVert_{W_{2}}\leq\left\lVert\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}(\boldsymbol{X})-\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime})\right\rVert_{W_{2}}, $$

where the last inequality is due to the contractivity of quantum Wasserstein distance under tensor product channels Anschuetz, 2026. So now, we have that

$$ \displaystyle\Pr_{(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime})\sim\Xi}\Bigg[\left\lVert\EE_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right|-\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right|\right]\right\rVert_{W_{2}}\leq \displaystyle\leq f+L\left\lVert\boldsymbol{X}-\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{1}\mid\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}(\boldsymbol{X})\Bigg]\geq \displaystyle\geq{} \displaystyle\Pr_{(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime})\sim\Xi}\left[\left\lVert\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}(\boldsymbol{X})-\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime})\right\rVert_{W_{2}}\leq f+L\left\lVert\boldsymbol{X}-\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{1}\mid\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}(\boldsymbol{X})\right]\geq 1-3p_{\mathrm{st}}, $$

which proves Equation 60. Now, we want to show the second claim. By Equation 61 and Equation 62, we have that

$$ \displaystyle\Pr_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[V\left(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right)\geq\frac{1}{3}(\gamma-\delta)E_{\ast}\right]= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\Pr_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[\Tr\left(3\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right)\geq(\gamma-\delta)E_{\ast}\right]\geq \displaystyle\geq{} \displaystyle\Pr_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[\Tr\left(3\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{M}}}(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}(\boldsymbol{X}),\omega)\right)-\Tr\left(\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}(\boldsymbol{X})\right)\geq-\delta E_{\ast}\right]\geq 1-p_{\mathrm{est}}. $$

So, Equation 63 holds. ∎

#### 3.1.2. Constructing Collectively Stable Solution Configurations

Now that we have an algorithm satisfying the weak stability condition, the next step of the proof proceeds as follows. We sample many independent outputs from the algorithm, taking a large enough number so that at least one is near-optimal with high probability, and we argue that these outputs satisfy a notion of “collective stability”: that is, they obey the Lipschitz property on average. We will first need this result on the properties of the $W_{2}$ distance:

#### Proposition 3.7 (From Anschuetz (2026, Proposition 29)).

For each problem instance $\boldsymbol{X}$ , let $p_{\boldsymbol{X}}(\mathbf{s})$ be the probability distribution of $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\in\{0,1\}^{n}$ over $\omega\sim\mathcal{U}$ . Then, for every pair of problem instances $\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime}$ , there exists some probability distribution $\pi_{\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{s}^{\prime})$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\EE_{\mathbf{s},\mathbf{s}^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime}}}\left[d_{\mathrm{H}}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{s}^{\prime})^{2}\right]\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\left\lVert\EE_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right|-\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right|\right]\right\rVert_{W_{2}}^{2}, $$

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{s}^{\prime}}\pi_{\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{s}^{\prime})=p_{\boldsymbol{X}}(\mathbf{s}), $$

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{s}}\pi_{\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{s}^{\prime})=p_{\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{s}^{\prime}). $$

#### Proof.

We can write

$$ \EE_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right|-\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right|\right]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\boldsymbol{A}_{i}, $$

where the $\boldsymbol{A}_{i}$ are Hermitian such that $\Tr_{\{i\}}\left(\boldsymbol{A}_{i}\right)=0$ , picked to be the optimal in Definition 2.7. Now, we can write each $\boldsymbol{A}_{i}$ as $\boldsymbol{A}_{i}^{+}-\boldsymbol{A}_{i}^{-}$ , where $\boldsymbol{A}_{i}^{+}$ and $\boldsymbol{A}_{i}^{-}$ are positive semidefinite with the same trace. So, we can write $\boldsymbol{A}_{i}=c_{i}\left(\boldsymbol{\rho}_{i}-\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{i}\right)$ , where $\boldsymbol{\rho}_{i}$ and $\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{i}$ are density matrices diagonal in the computational basis, where

$$ c_{i}=\left\lVert\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{A}_{i}\right\rVert_{\ast}=\Tr\left(\boldsymbol{A}_{i}^{+}\right)=\Tr\left(\boldsymbol{A}_{i}^{-}\right). $$

Then, we have that

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sqrt{c_{i}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sqrt{\left\lVert\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{A}_{i}\right\rVert_{\ast}}= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\left\lVert\EE_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right|-\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right|\right]\right\rVert_{W_{2}}. $$

Since the density matrices $\boldsymbol{\rho}_{i}$ and $\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{i}$ are diagonal in the computational basis, we can write $p_{i},q_{i}$ for their diagonals (representing probability distributions over bit strings), respectively. Similarly, write $p,q$ for the diagonal elements of $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ , $\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ . Observe that the marginals of $p_{i}$ and $q_{i}$ on $[n]\setminus\{i\}$ are the same, which means that $W_{2}(p_{i},q_{i})\leq 1$ . Thus, we have that

$$ \displaystyle\inf_{\pi_{\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{C}\left(p_{\boldsymbol{X}},p_{\boldsymbol{X^{\prime}}}\right)}\EE_{\mathbf{s},\mathbf{s}^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime}}}\left[d_{\mathrm{H}}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{s}^{\prime})^{2}\right]=W_{2}\left(p,q\right)^{2}\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sqrt{c_{i}}W_{2}(p_{i},q_{i})\right)^{2}\leq\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sqrt{c_{i}}\right)^{2}= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\left\lVert\EE_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right|-\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right|\right]\right\rVert_{W_{2}}^{2}. $$

∎

#### Lemma 3.8 (From Anschuetz (2026, Lemma 30)).

Let $\Xi$ be a probability distribution of pairs of problem instances on the same hypergraph whose marginal distributions are both $\Lambda$ . Fix $\beta>0$ and $R\in\mathbb{N}$ such that

$$ \frac{1}{\beta^{2}}+p_{\mathrm{est}}^{R}<1. $$

Then, with probability at least $1-3p_{\mathrm{st}}-3p_{\mathrm{f}}-p_{\mathrm{b}}$ over $(\hat{\boldsymbol{X}},\boldsymbol{X})\sim\Xi$ , conditioned on the event $\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{X}}\right)$ , there exists a set of bit strings $\left(\hat{\mathbf{s}}^{(r)},\mathbf{s}^{(r)}\in\{0,1\}^{n}\right)_{r\in[R]}$ such that we have a “collective stability” condition:

$$ \frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}d_{\mathrm{H}}\left(\hat{\mathbf{s}}^{(r)},\mathbf{s}^{(r)}\right)\leq\beta f+\beta L\left\lVert\hat{\boldsymbol{X}}-\boldsymbol{X}\right\rVert_{1}, $$

and

$$ \max_{r\in[R]}V\left(\boldsymbol{X},\mathbf{s}^{(r)}\right)\geq\frac{1}{3}(\gamma-\delta)E_{\ast}. $$

#### Proof.

Consider some $\hat{\boldsymbol{X}},\boldsymbol{X}$ that satisfies the following conditions:

$$ \left\lVert\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{X}})-\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}(\boldsymbol{X})\right\rVert_{W_{2}}\leq f+L\left\lVert\hat{\boldsymbol{X}}-\boldsymbol{X}\right\rVert_{1}, $$

$$ \Tr\left(\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}(\boldsymbol{X})\right)\geq\gamma E_{\ast}, $$

$$ \Pr_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[\Tr\left(3\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{M}}}(\boldsymbol{\rho},\omega)\right)-\Tr\left(\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\boldsymbol{\rho}\right)\geq-\delta E_{\ast}\right]\geq 1-p_{\mathrm{est}}\quad\forall\boldsymbol{\rho}\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{m}}_{n}. $$

By the union bound, the probability over $\Xi$ that all of these conditions occur is at least

$$ 1-3p_{\mathrm{st}}-3p_{\mathrm{f}}-p_{\mathrm{b}}. $$

Let $p_{\hat{\boldsymbol{X}}},p_{\boldsymbol{X}}$ be the probability distributions of $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{X}},\omega)$ and $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)$ , respectively, over $\omega\sim\mathcal{U}$ , and let $\pi_{\hat{\boldsymbol{X}},\boldsymbol{X}}$ be the joint distribution as in Proposition 3.7. We then have that when $\hat{\boldsymbol{X}},\boldsymbol{X}$ satisfy the above conditions, by Lemma 3.6 and Proposition 3.7, we have that

$$ \displaystyle\EE_{\left(\hat{\mathbf{s}},\mathbf{s}\right)\sim\pi}\left[d_{\mathrm{H}}\left(\hat{\mathbf{s}},\mathbf{s}\right)^{2}\right]\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\left\lVert\EE_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{X}},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{X}},\omega)\right|-\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right|\right]\right\rVert_{W_{2}}^{2}\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\left(f+L\left\lVert\hat{\boldsymbol{X}}-\boldsymbol{X}\right\rVert_{1}\right)^{2}. $$

We will now use this distribution to sample $R$ many independent replicas from the algorithm $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}$ (the shadows estimator applied to $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}$ ), and show that they satisfy the desired conditions.

By Markov’s inequality,

$$ \displaystyle\Pr_{\left(\hat{\mathbf{s}}^{(r)},\mathbf{s}^{(r)}\right)_{r\in[R]}\sim\pi_{\hat{\boldsymbol{X}},\boldsymbol{X}}^{\times R}}\left[\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}d_{\mathrm{H}}\left(\hat{\mathbf{s}}^{(r)},\mathbf{s}^{(r)}\right)>\beta\left(f+L\left\lVert\hat{\boldsymbol{X}}-\boldsymbol{X}\right\rVert_{1}\right)\right]= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\Pr_{\left(\hat{\mathbf{s}}^{(r)},\mathbf{s}^{(r)}\right)_{r\in[R]}\sim\pi_{\hat{\boldsymbol{X}},\boldsymbol{X}}^{\times R}}\left[\left(\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}d_{\mathrm{H}}\left(\hat{\mathbf{s}}^{(r)},\mathbf{s}^{(r)}\right)\right)^{2}>\beta^{2}\left(f+L\left\lVert\hat{\boldsymbol{X}}-\boldsymbol{X}\right\rVert_{1}\right)^{2}\right]\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\frac{\EE_{\left(\hat{\mathbf{s}}^{(r)},\mathbf{s}^{(r)}\right)_{r\in[R]}\sim\pi_{\hat{\boldsymbol{X}},\boldsymbol{X}}^{\times R}}\left[\left(\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}d_{\mathrm{H}}\left(\hat{\mathbf{s}}^{(r)},\mathbf{s}^{(r)}\right)\right)^{2}\right]}{\beta^{2}\left(f+L\left\lVert\hat{\boldsymbol{X}}-\boldsymbol{X}\right\rVert_{1}\right)^{2}}\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\frac{\EE_{\left(\hat{\mathbf{s}},\mathbf{s}\right)\sim\pi_{\hat{\boldsymbol{X}},\boldsymbol{X}}}\left[d_{\mathrm{H}}\left(\hat{\mathbf{s}},\mathbf{s}\right)^{2}\right]}{\beta^{2}\left(f+L\left\lVert\hat{\boldsymbol{X}}-\boldsymbol{X}\right\rVert_{1}\right)^{2}}\leq\frac{1}{\beta^{2}}. $$

Now, from Lemma 3.6, for our choice of $\hat{\boldsymbol{X}},\boldsymbol{X}$ , we also have that

$$ \Pr_{\mathbf{s}\sim p_{\boldsymbol{X}}}\left[V\left(\boldsymbol{X},\mathbf{s}\right)<\frac{1}{3}(\gamma-\delta)E_{\ast}\right]=\Pr_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[V\left(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right)<\frac{1}{3}(\gamma-\delta)E_{\ast}\right]\leq p_{\mathrm{est}}. $$

So, since the replicas are sampled independently, we have that

$$ \Pr_{\left(\hat{\mathbf{s}}^{(r)},\mathbf{s}^{(r)}\right)_{r\in[R]}\sim\pi_{\hat{\boldsymbol{X}},\boldsymbol{X}}^{\times R}}\left[\max_{r\in[R]}V\left(\boldsymbol{X},\mathbf{s}^{(r)}\right)<\frac{1}{3}(\gamma-\delta)E_{\ast}\right]\leq p_{\mathrm{est}}^{R}. $$

Since we chose $\beta,R$ such that

$$ \frac{1}{\beta^{2}}+p_{\mathrm{est}}^{R}<1, $$

there must exist $\left(\mathbf{s}^{(r)}\in\{0,1\}^{n}\right)_{r\in[R]}$ such that the desired conditions are satisfied. ∎

#### 3.1.3. Taking Many Correlated Problem Instances

We now extend the above results to many problem instances that are highly correlated with each other, with each one only resampling hyperedges adjacent to a small fraction $F$ of the qubits. This is a simplified version of the interpolation path typically seen in OGP proofs (and which we will see in Section 4). Here, instead of constructing a full interpolation path, we are effectively only taking a single step along it. It is important to note that we do not lose much by doing this: because of the way the collectively stable configurations are constructed, using a full interpolation path does not allow us to prove stronger results. We explain this limitation in more detail in Section 5.2.

#### Definition 3.9.

For $m\in\mathbb{N}$ and $F\in(0,1]$ , we define the distribution $\Xi_{F,m}$ of collections $\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{X}},\boldsymbol{X}^{(1)},\dots,\boldsymbol{X}^{(m)}\right)$ as follows. First, sample $\boldsymbol{S}$ by setting each $S_{A}\sim\Bern\left(p/\binom{n-1}{p-1}\right)$ i.i.d. Then, sample $\hat{\boldsymbol{J}},\widetilde{\boldsymbol{J}}^{(1)},\dots,\widetilde{\boldsymbol{J}}^{(m)}$ with i.i.d. entries in $\{-1,1\}$ . Then, for all and $A\in\binom{[n]}{k}$ , set $\boldsymbol{X}$

$$ X^{(t)}_{A}=\begin{cases}S_{A}\widetilde{J}^{(t)}_{A}&\text{ if }A\cap\left[\left\lceil Fn\right\rceil\right]\neq\varnothing\\
S_{A}\hat{J}_{A}&\text{ otherwise. }\end{cases} $$

In other words, we are interpolating between $\hat{\boldsymbol{X}}$ and $m$ other problem instances on the same hypergraph with independent weights by resampling the weights of hyperedges intersecting with the first $F$ fraction of qubits. We call the marginal distribution of $\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{X}},\boldsymbol{X}^{(t)}\right)$ for a fixed $t$ by the name $\Xi_{F}$ . Observe that these marginal distributions are independent of $t$ .

#### Lemma 3.10.

Suppose that there exists a quantum algorithm $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}$ that is $\left(f,L,\mathfrak{d},\Xi_{F},p_{\mathrm{st}}\right)$ -stable and $(\gamma,p_{\mathrm{f}})$ -optimal for $\QMC(n,k,p)$ . Let $\beta$ be such that

$$ \frac{m}{\beta^{2}}+mp_{\mathrm{est}}^{R}<1. $$

Then, with probability at least

$$ 1-3mp_{\mathrm{st}}-3mp_{\mathrm{f}}-mp_{\mathrm{b}} $$

over $\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{X}},\boldsymbol{X}^{(1)},\dots,\boldsymbol{X}^{(m)}\right)\sim\Xi_{F,m}$ , conditioned on $\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{X}}\right)$ , there exist bit strings $\hat{\mathbf{s}}^{(r)}$ , $\mathbf{s}^{(t,r)}$ for $t\in[m]$ , $r\in[R]$ such that for all $t\in[m]$ we have that

$$ \frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}d_{\mathrm{H}}\left(\hat{\mathbf{s}},\mathbf{s}^{(t,r)}\right)\leq\beta f+\beta L\left\lVert\hat{\boldsymbol{X}}-\boldsymbol{X}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{1}, $$

and

$$ \max_{r\in[R]}V\left(\boldsymbol{X}^{(t)},\mathbf{s}^{(t,r)}\right)\geq\frac{1}{3}\left(\gamma-\delta\right)E_{\ast}. $$

#### Proof.

Fix $\hat{\boldsymbol{X}},\boldsymbol{X}^{(1)},\dots,\boldsymbol{X}^{(m)}$ such that for each $t\in[m]$ , $\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{X}},\boldsymbol{X}^{(t)}\right)$ satisfies the condition in the proof of Lemma 3.8. Then, by the union bound, this occurs with probability of at least $1-3mp_{\mathrm{st}}-3mp_{\mathrm{f}}-mp_{\mathrm{b}}$ over $\Xi_{F,m}$ . Then, applying a union bound to the argument in Lemma 3.8, we have that

$$ \displaystyle\Pr_{\left(\hat{\mathbf{s}}^{(r)},\mathbf{s}^{(0,r)},\dots,\mathbf{s}^{(m,r)}\right)_{r\in[R]}\sim\left(\Xi_{F,m}\right)^{\times R}} \displaystyle\left[\max_{t\in[m]}\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}d_{\mathrm{H}}\left(\hat{\mathbf{s}}^{(r)},\mathbf{s}^{(r)}\right)>\beta\left(f+L\left\lVert\hat{\boldsymbol{X}}-\boldsymbol{X}\right\rVert_{1}\right)\right]\leq\frac{m}{\beta^{2}} $$

and

$$ \Pr_{\left(\hat{\mathbf{s}}^{(r)},\mathbf{s}^{(r)}\right)_{r\in[R]}\sim\pi_{\hat{\boldsymbol{X}},\boldsymbol{X}}^{\times R}}\left[\min_{t\in[m]}\max_{r\in[R]}V\left(\boldsymbol{X},\mathbf{s}^{(r)}\right)<\frac{1}{3}(\gamma-\delta)E_{\ast}\right]\leq mp_{\mathrm{est}}^{R}. $$

Since $m/\beta^{2}+mp_{\mathrm{est}}^{R}<1$ , this completes the proof. ∎

#### Lemma 3.11.

If $\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime}$ are $d$ -dimensional vectors sampled by first setting each entry to $0$ in both vectors with probability $1-p$ and then setting the remaining entries to $-1$ or $1$ independently, we have that

$$ \Pr\left[\left\lVert\boldsymbol{X}-\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{1}\geq 3pd\right]\leq e^{-pd(3\log 2-2)}. $$

#### Proof.

$$ \displaystyle\Pr\left[\left\lVert\boldsymbol{X}-\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{1}>t\right]=\Pr\left[e^{\alpha\left\lVert\boldsymbol{X}-\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{1}}>e^{\alpha t}\right]\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle e^{-\alpha t}\EE\left[e^{\alpha\left\lVert\boldsymbol{X}-\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{1}}\right]=e^{-\alpha t}\left(\frac{p}{2}e^{2\alpha}+1-\frac{p}{2}\right)^{d}\leq \displaystyle={} \displaystyle e^{-\alpha t}\left(1+\frac{p}{2}e^{2\alpha}\right)^{d}\leq e^{-\alpha t}e^{\frac{1}{2}pde^{2\alpha}}. $$

If we take $\alpha=\log 2$ and $t=3pd$ , this becomes

$$ \Pr\left[\left\lVert\boldsymbol{X}-\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{1}>3pd\right]\leq e^{2pd-3pd\log 2}=e^{-pd(3\log 2-2)}. $$

∎

#### Lemma 3.12.

Suppose that there exists a quantum algorithm $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}$ that is $\left(f,L,\Xi_{F},p_{\mathrm{st}}\right)$ -stable and $(\gamma,p_{\mathrm{f}})$ -optimal for $\QMC(n,k,p)$ . Let $\beta$ be such that

$$ \frac{m}{\beta^{2}}+mp_{\mathrm{est}}^{R}<1. $$

Then, with probability at least

$$ 1-3mp_{\mathrm{st}}-3mp_{\mathrm{f}}-mp_{\mathrm{b}}-me^{-pFn(3\log 2-2)} $$

over $\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{X}},\boldsymbol{X}^{(1)},\dots,\boldsymbol{X}^{(T)}\right)\sim\Xi_{F,m}$ , conditioned on $\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{X}}\right)$ , there exist bit strings $\mathbf{s}^{(t,r)}$ for $t\in[m]$ , $r\in[R]$ such that for all $t\neq t^{\prime}\in[m]$ ,

$$ \frac{1}{Rn}\sum_{r=1}^{R}d_{\mathrm{H}}\left(\mathbf{s}^{(t,r)},\mathbf{s}^{(t^{\prime},r)}\right)\leq\frac{2\beta f}{n}+6\beta LpF, $$

and for all $t\in[m]$ ,

$$ \max_{r\in[R]}V\left(\boldsymbol{X}^{(t)},\mathbf{s}^{(t,r)}\right)\geq\frac{1}{3}\left(\gamma-\delta\right)E_{\ast}. $$

#### Proof.

Observe that $\hat{X}^{(t)}_{A}$ can be different from $X^{(t)}_{A}$ only if we have $A\cap[\left\lceil Fn\right\rceil]\neq\varnothing$ . Since $A$ must contain one of $Fn$ many qubits, the number of such $A$ is at most

$$ Fn\binom{n-1}{k-1}. $$

Then,

$$ \frac{p}{\binom{n-1}{k-1}}\cdot Fn\binom{n-1}{k-1}=pFn. $$

So, by Lemma 3.11, we have that

$$ \Pr_{\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{X}},\boldsymbol{X}^{(1)},\dots,\boldsymbol{X}^{(m)}\right)\sim\Xi_{F,m}}\left[\max_{t\in[m]}\left\lVert\hat{\boldsymbol{X}}-\boldsymbol{X}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{1}\leq 3pFn\right]\geq 1-me^{-pFn(3\log 2-2)} $$

Suppose that this event and the event from Lemma 3.10 (which occurs with probability $\geq 1-3mp_{\mathrm{st}}-3mp_{\mathrm{f}}-mp_{\mathrm{b}}$ conditioned on $\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{X}}\right)$ . Then, for all $t\in[m]$ , we have that

$$ \max_{r\in[R]}V\left(\boldsymbol{X}^{(t)},\mathbf{s}^{(t,r)}\right)\geq\frac{1}{3}\left(\gamma-\delta\right)E_{\ast}, $$

and for $t\neq t^{\prime}$ , we have that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}d_{\mathrm{H}}\left(\mathbf{s}^{(t,r)},\mathbf{s}^{(t^{\prime},r)}\right)\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle 2\beta f+\beta L\left(\left\lVert\hat{\boldsymbol{X}}-\boldsymbol{X}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert\hat{\boldsymbol{X}}-\boldsymbol{X}^{(t^{\prime})}\right\rVert_{1}\right)\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle 2\beta f+6\beta LpFn, $$

so

$$ \frac{1}{Rn}\sum_{r=1}^{R}d_{\mathrm{H}}\left(\mathbf{s}^{(t,r)},\mathbf{s}^{(t^{\prime},r)}\right)\leq\frac{2\beta f}{n}+6\beta LpF. $$

∎

#### 3.1.4. Lower Bound on the Probability of Bounded Degree

In the previous calculations, we have been conditioning on the event $\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}(\boldsymbol{S})$ that our hypergraph has maximum degree bounded by a constant $\mathfrak{d}$ . In this section, we lower-bound the probability of this event for our distribution of problem instances (where each vertex in the hypergraph has expected degree $p$ ).

#### Proposition 3.13.

Suppose that each $S_{A}$ for $A\in\binom{[n]}{k}$ is i.i.d. $\Bern\left(p/\binom{n-1}{k-1}\right)$ . Then,

$$ \Pr\left[\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}(\boldsymbol{S})\right]\geq\left(1-\left(\frac{e\mathfrak{d}}{p}\right)^{\mathfrak{d}}e^{-p}\right)^{n}. $$

#### Proof.

For $v\in[n]$ , let $D_{v}$ be the degree of $v$ in the hypergraph. We have that $\EE\left[D_{v}\right]=p$ . Then, we have that

$$ \displaystyle\Pr\left[D_{v}>d\right]=\Pr\left[e^{\alpha D_{v}}>e^{\alpha d}\right]\leq e^{-\alpha\mathfrak{d}}\EE\left[e^{\alpha D_{v}}\right]= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle e^{-\alpha\mathfrak{d}}\left(\frac{p}{\binom{n-1}{k-1}}e^{\alpha}+1-\frac{p}{\binom{n-1}{k-1}}\right)^{\binom{n-1}{k-1}}=e^{-\alpha\mathfrak{d}}\left(1+\frac{p}{\binom{n-1}{k-1}}(e^{\alpha}-1)\right)^{\binom{n-1}{k-1}}\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle e^{-\alpha\mathfrak{d}+p(e^{\alpha}-1)}. $$

Optimizing for $\alpha$ , we must have $-\mathfrak{d}+pe^{\alpha}=0$ , so $\alpha=\log(\mathfrak{d}/p)$ , so

$$ \Pr\left[D_{v}>\mathfrak{d}\right]\leq e^{-\mathfrak{d}\log(\mathfrak{d}/p)+\mathfrak{d}-p}=\left(\frac{p}{\mathfrak{d}}\right)^{\mathfrak{d}}e^{\mathfrak{d}-p}=\left(\frac{ep}{\mathfrak{d}}\right)^{\mathfrak{d}}e^{-p}. $$

Now, observe that

$$ \Pr\left[\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}(\boldsymbol{S})\right]=\Pr\left[D_{v}\leq\mathfrak{d}\;\forall v\in[n]\right]\geq\prod_{v\in[n]}\Pr\left[D_{v}\leq\mathfrak{d}\right]\geq\left(1-\left(\frac{ep}{\mathfrak{d}}\right)^{\mathfrak{d}}e^{-p}\right)^{n}. $$

∎

#### Corollary 3.14.

For any $0<\epsilon\leq\log 2$ , if we let

$$ \mathfrak{d}\geq\left\lceil\max\left(e^{2}p,2\log(1/\epsilon)\right)\right\rceil, $$

then

$$ \Pr\left[\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}\left(\boldsymbol{S}\right)\right]\geq e^{-\epsilon n}. $$

#### Proof.

By Proposition 3.13, we have that

$$ \Pr\left[\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}(\boldsymbol{S})\right]\geq\left(1-\left(\frac{ep}{\mathfrak{d}}\right)^{\mathfrak{d}}e^{-p}\right)^{n}\geq\left(1-e^{-2\log(1/\epsilon)}e^{-p}\right)^{n}\geq(1-\epsilon^{2})^{n}\geq e^{-\epsilon n}. $$

∎

### 3.2. Non-Existence of Forbidden Configurations

In this section, we will demonstrate a (simplified version of) the QOGP. We will argue that the set of “forbidden configurations” of solution bit strings is empty with high probability, contradicting the above argument showing the existence of these configurations if a stable algorithm exists. This ultimately allows us to prove the weak hardness result for stable algorithms.

#### 3.2.1. Entropy Bound

#### Definition 3.15.

Let

$$ \mathcal{F}(n,m,R,\xi)\coloneq\left\{\left(\mathbf{s}^{(t,r)}\in\{0,1\}^{n}\right)_{t\in[m],r\in[R]}:\frac{1}{Rn}\sum_{r=1}^{R}d_{\mathrm{H}}\left(\mathbf{s}^{(t,r)},\mathbf{s}^{(t^{\prime},r)}\right)\leq\xi\right\}. $$

#### Lemma 3.16.

$$ \left\lvert\mathcal{F}(n,m,R,\xi)\right\rvert\leq\exp\left[n\cdot\left(R\log 2+(m-1)R\entropy(\xi)\right)(1+o_{n}(1))\right]. $$

#### Proof.

Let $\mathbf{s}^{(t)}\coloneq\left(\mathbf{s}^{(t,r)}\right)_{r\in[R]}$ . Then,

$$ \frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}d_{\mathrm{H}}\left(\mathbf{s}^{(t,r)},\mathbf{s}^{(t^{\prime},r)}\right)\leq\xi n\iff d_{\mathrm{H}}\left(\mathbf{s}^{(t)},\mathbf{s}^{(t^{\prime})}\right)\leq\xi Rn. $$

If we fix $\mathbf{s}^{(t)}$ , then the number of $\mathbf{s}^{(t^{\prime})}$ that satisfy this is at most

$$ \sum_{j=0}^{\left\lfloor\xi Rn\right\rfloor}\binom{Rn}{j}\leq Rn\binom{Rn}{\xi Rn}=\exp\left[Rn\entropy(\xi)(1+o_{n}(1))\right]. $$

Now, considering all $m-1$ choices of $t^{\prime}$ and the $2^{Rn}=\exp\left(Rn\log 2\right)$ , we have that

$$ \left\lvert\mathcal{F}(n,m,R,\xi)\right\rvert\leq\exp\left[n\cdot\left(R\log 2+(m-1)R\entropy(\xi)\right)(1+o_{n}(1))\right]. $$

∎

#### 3.2.2. Covariance Bound

Now, take some $\left(\mathbf{s}^{(t,r)}\right)_{t\in[m],r\in[R]}\in\mathcal{F}(n,m,R,\xi)$ . We can write

$$ \displaystyle\Pr_{\boldsymbol{X}^{(1)},\dots,\boldsymbol{X}^{(m)}\sim\Xi_{F,m}}\left[\min_{t\in[m]}\max_{r\in[R]}V\left(\boldsymbol{X}^{(t)},\mathbf{s}^{(t,r)}\right)\geq\alpha\right]\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle R^{m}\max_{(r_{t})_{t\in[m]}}\Pr_{\boldsymbol{X}^{(1)},\dots,\boldsymbol{X}^{(m)}\sim\Xi_{F,m}}\left[\min_{t\in[m]}V\left(\boldsymbol{X}^{(t)},\mathbf{s}^{(t,r_{t})}\right)\geq\alpha\right]. $$

Now, we have that

$$ \EE\left[V\left(\boldsymbol{X}^{(t)},\mathbf{s}^{(t,r_{t})}\right)\right]=0, $$

and also, as in the proof of Theorem 2.6, we have

$$ \displaystyle\EE\left[V\left(\boldsymbol{X}^{(t)},\mathbf{s}^{(t,r_{t})}\right)^{2}\right]=\frac{p}{n}, $$

and for $t\neq t^{\prime}$ , we have that

$$ \displaystyle\EE\left[V\left(\boldsymbol{X}^{(t)},\mathbf{s}^{(t,r_{t})}\right)V\left(\boldsymbol{X}^{(t^{\prime})},\mathbf{s}^{(t^{\prime},r_{t^{\prime}})}\right)\right]= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\frac{k}{n^{2}}\sum_{A,A^{\prime}\in\binom{[n]}{k}}\EE\left[X^{(t)}_{A}\boldsymbol{X}^{(t^{\prime})}_{A^{\prime}}\right](-1)^{\sum_{v\in A}\boldsymbol{s}^{(t,r_{t})}_{v}+\sum_{v^{\prime}\in A^{\prime}}\boldsymbol{s}^{(t^{\prime},r_{t^{\prime}})}_{v^{\prime}}}= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\frac{k}{n^{2}}\sum_{A\in\binom{[n]}{k}}\EE\left[X^{(t)}_{A}X^{(t^{\prime})}_{A}\right](-1)^{\sum_{v\in A}\left(\boldsymbol{s}^{(t,r_{t})}_{v}+\boldsymbol{s}^{(t^{\prime},r_{t^{\prime}})}_{v}\right)}= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\frac{kp}{n^{2}\binom{n-1}{k-1}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\in\binom{[n]}{k}\\
A\cap[\left\lceil Fn\right\rceil]=\varnothing\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\sum_{v\in A}\left(\boldsymbol{s}^{(t,r_{t})}_{v}+\boldsymbol{s}^{(t^{\prime},r_{t^{\prime}})}_{v}\right)}\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\frac{kp}{n^{2}\binom{n-1}{k-1}}\binom{\left\lfloor(1-F)n\right\rfloor}{k}= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\frac{kp}{n^{2}}\frac{(k-1)!}{n^{k-1}}\frac{(1-F)^{k}n^{k}}{k!}(1+o_{n}(1))= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\frac{p}{n}(1-F)^{k}(1+o_{n}(1)). $$

Now, consider the $m\times m$ covariance matrix

$$ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\frac{p}{n}\left[\left(1-(1-F)^{k}\right)\Id_{m}+(1-F)^{k}\boldsymbol{J}_{m}\right] $$

where $\boldsymbol{J}_{m}$ is the $m\times m$ matrix consisting of all ones. We know that the eigenvalues of $\boldsymbol{J}_{m}$ are $m$ (with multiplicity $1$ ) and $0$ (with multiplicity $m-1$ ). So, the eigenvalues of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ are:

$$ \sigma_{1}\coloneq\frac{p}{n}\left(1+(m-1)(1-F)^{k}\right)\qquad\text{(with multiplicity 1)}, $$

and

$$ \sigma_{2}\coloneq\frac{p}{n}\left(1-(1-F)^{k}\right)\leq\sigma_{1}\qquad\text{(with multiplicity $m-1$)}. $$

So, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is positive definite and invertible. We then have that

$$ \left\lVert\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\sigma_{2}^{-1/2}=\sqrt{\frac{n}{p\left(1-(1-F)^{k}\right)}}. $$

We can think of $\left\{\overline{X}_{A}\right\}_{A\in\binom{[n]}{k}}$ as a set of $\binom{n}{k}$ $m$ -dimensional independent vectors with an entry for each $t\in[m]$ corresponding to the contribution to $V\left(\boldsymbol{X}^{(t)},\mathbf{s}^{(t,r_{t})}\right)$ from the $X^{(t)}_{A}$ term. Then, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is the covariance matrix of the sum of these vectors (which is the $m$ -dimensional vector of $V\left(\boldsymbol{X}^{(t)},\mathbf{s}^{(t,r_{t})}\right)$ over $t\in[m]$ ). By the Berry-Esseen Theorem Raič, 2019, if we take an $m$ -dimensional Gaussian vector $G=\left(G^{(t)}\right)_{t\in[m]}$ with mean $0$ and covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ , then we have that

$$ \displaystyle\Pr_{\boldsymbol{X}^{(1)},\dots,\boldsymbol{X}^{(m)}\sim\Xi_{F,m}}\left[\min_{t\in[m]}V\left(\boldsymbol{X}^{(t)},\mathbf{s}^{(t,r_{t})}\right)\geq\alpha\right]\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\Pr\left[\min_{t\in[m]}G^{(t)}\geq\alpha\right]+Cm^{1/4}\sum_{A\in\binom{[n]}{k}}\EE\left[\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\overline{X}_{A}\right\rVert_{2}^{3}\right], $$

where $C$ is some universal constant. Now, we have that

$$ \displaystyle\EE\left[\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\overline{X}_{A}\right\rVert_{2}^{3}\right]\leq\left(\frac{n}{p\left(1-(1-F)^{k}\right)}\right)^{3/2}\EE\left[\left\lVert\overline{X}_{A}\right\rVert_{2}^{3}\right]\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\left(\frac{n}{p\left(1-(1-F)^{k}\right)}\right)^{3/2}\frac{\sqrt{k}}{n}\EE\left[\left\lVert\overline{X}_{A}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right]= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\frac{\sqrt{kn}}{\left(p\left(1-(1-F)^{k}\right)\right)^{3/2}}\sum_{t\in[m]}\EE\left[\left(\overline{X_{A}}\right)_{t}^{2}\right]= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\frac{\sqrt{kn}}{\left(p\left(1-p(1-F)^{k}\right)\right)^{3/2}}\frac{mp}{\binom{n-1}{k-1}}\frac{k}{n^{2}}= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\left(\frac{k}{n\left(1-(1-F)^{k}\right)}\right)^{3/2}\frac{m}{\sqrt{p}\binom{n-1}{k-1}}. $$

Thus,

$$ \displaystyle\Pr_{\boldsymbol{X}^{(1)},\dots,\boldsymbol{X}^{(m)}\sim\Xi_{F,m}}\left[\min_{t\in[m]}V\left(\boldsymbol{X}^{(t)},\mathbf{s}^{(t,r_{t})}\right)\geq\alpha\right]\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\Pr\left[\min_{t\in[m]}G^{(t)}\geq\alpha\right]+Cm^{1/4}\binom{n}{k}\left(\frac{k}{n\left(1-(1-F)^{k}\right)}\right)^{3/2}\frac{m}{\sqrt{p}\binom{n-1}{k-1}}= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\Pr\left[\min_{t\in[m]}G^{(t)}\geq\alpha\right]+\frac{Cm^{5/4}}{\sqrt{p}}\frac{n}{k}\left(\frac{k}{n\left(1-(1-F)^{k}\right)}\right)^{3/2}= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\Pr\left[\min_{t\in[m]}G^{(t)}\geq\alpha\right]+\frac{Cm^{5/4}}{\left(1-(1-F)^{k}\right)^{3/2}}\sqrt{\frac{k}{pn}}= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\Pr\left[\min_{t\in[m]}G^{(t)}\geq\alpha\right]+o_{n}(1). $$

Now that we have a bound in terms of Gaussians, we can write, up to $o_{n}(1)$ terms,

$$ \displaystyle\Pr_{\boldsymbol{X}^{(1)},\dots,\boldsymbol{X}^{(m)}\sim\Xi_{F,m}}\left[\min_{t\in[m]}\max_{r\in[R]}V\left(\boldsymbol{X}^{(t)},\mathbf{s}^{(t,r)}\right)\geq\alpha\right]\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle R^{m}\Pr\left[\min_{t\in[m]}G^{(t)}\geq\alpha\right]\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle R^{m}\Pr\left[\sum_{t\in[m]}G^{(t)}\geq m\alpha\right]\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\exp\left[m\log R-\frac{\frac{1}{2}m^{2}\alpha^{2}}{\frac{mp}{n}+\frac{m(m-1)p}{n}(1-F)^{k}}\right]= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\exp\left[-\frac{\frac{1}{2p}nm\alpha^{2}}{1+(m-1)(1-F)^{k}}\right](1+o_{n}(1)). $$

So now, by the first moment method, we have that

$$ \displaystyle\Pr_{\boldsymbol{X}^{(1)},\dots,\boldsymbol{X}^{(m)}\sim\Xi_{F,m}}\left[\max_{\left(\mathbf{s}^{(t,r)}\right)_{t\in[m],r\in[R]}\in\mathcal{F}(n,m,R,\xi)}\min_{t\in[m]}\max_{r\in[R]}V\left(\boldsymbol{X}^{(t)},\mathbf{s}^{(t,r)}\right)\geq\alpha\right]\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\exp\left[n\left(R\log 2+(m-1)R\entropy(\xi)-\frac{\frac{1}{2p}m\alpha^{2}}{1+(m-1)(1-F)^{k}}\right)(1+o_{n}(1))\right]. $$

If the expression above is $\geq 2^{-n}$ , we must have that

$$ \alpha^{2}\leq\frac{2p}{m}\left((R+1)\log 2+(m-1)R\entropy(\xi)\right)\left(1+(m-1)(1-F)^{k}\right). $$

Note that an extra $\log 2$ term is added to account for the desired $2^{-n}$ bound. Now, if we pick

$$ \beta=\sqrt{\frac{m}{0.99-mp_{\mathrm{est}}^{R}}} $$

to satisfy $m/\beta^{2}+mp_{\mathrm{est}}^{R}<1$ , and

$$ \xi=\frac{2\beta f}{n}+6\beta LpF=\sqrt{\frac{m}{0.99-mp_{\mathrm{est}}^{R}}}\left(\frac{2f}{n}+6LpF\right), $$

then, substituting $p_{\mathrm{est}}$ from Lemma 2.16, we have (assuming that $f=o(n)$ ),

$$ \entropy(\xi)\leq\sqrt{2\xi}=2\left(\frac{m}{0.99-\frac{m}{\left(1+0.99\cdot\delta^{2}/9\right)^{R}}}\right)^{1/4}\sqrt{3LpF}(1+o_{n}(1)). $$

#### 3.2.3. Completing the Proof

We now want to get a contradiction with Lemma 3.12. To do this, we can show that for any $0<\gamma\leq 1$ and $L\geq 0$ , there exists some choice of $R,m,F,k,\delta$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{2p}{m}\left((R+1)\log 2+2(m-1)R\left(\frac{m}{0.99-\frac{m}{\left(1+0.99\cdot\delta^{2}/9\right)^{R}}}\right)^{1/4}\sqrt{3LpF}\right)\cdot \displaystyle\cdot\left(1+(m-1)(1-F)^{k}\right)< \displaystyle<{} \displaystyle\frac{2p}{9}(\gamma-\delta)^{2}\log 2\leq\left(\frac{1}{3}(\gamma-\delta)E_{\ast}^{(k)}\right)^{2}, $$

that is,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{m}\left((R+1)\log 2+\frac{2(m-1)R\sqrt{3LpF}}{\left(\frac{0.99}{m}-\frac{1}{\left(1+0.99\cdot\delta^{2}/9\right)^{R}}\right)^{1/4}}\right)\left(1+(m-1)(1-F)^{k}\right)< \displaystyle<{} \displaystyle\frac{1}{9}(\gamma-\delta)^{2}\log 2. $$

To accomplish this, it is sufficient to first take $\delta=\gamma/2$ and pick $R,m,F,k$ to satisfy the following conditions:

$$ \frac{1}{m}(R+1)\log 2\leq\frac{1}{108}\gamma^{2}\log 2 $$

$$ \frac{2R\sqrt{3LpF}}{\left(\frac{0.99}{m}-\frac{1}{\left(1+0.99\cdot\gamma^{2}/36\right)^{R}}\right)^{1/4}}\leq\frac{1}{108}\gamma^{2}\log 2 $$

$$ 1+(m-1)(1-F)^{k}\leq\frac{3}{2} $$

Note that $(\gamma-\delta)^{2}=\gamma^{2}/4$ and we remove the factor of $(m-1)/m$ in the second condition.

To satisfy the first condition, we must have

$$ m\geq\left\lceil\frac{108}{\gamma^{2}}(R+1)\right\rceil. $$

Suppose we set $m$ to be exactly that value. Now, we want to set $R$ so that the denominator in the second condition is well-defined and positive. We want

$$ \frac{0.99}{m}>\frac{1}{(1+0.99\cdot\gamma^{2}/36)^{R}} $$

$$ \left(1+\frac{0.99\cdot\gamma^{2}}{36}\right)^{R}>\frac{m}{0.99}, $$

so it is sufficient to show that

$$ \left(1+\frac{0.99\cdot\gamma^{2}}{36}\right)^{R}>\frac{\frac{108}{\gamma^{2}}(R+1)+1}{0.99}=\frac{108}{0.99\cdot\gamma^{2}}(R+1)+1/0.99 $$

If we let $z=0.99\cdot\gamma^{2}/36$ , this is the same as

$$ (1+z)^{R}>\frac{3(R+1)}{z}+1/0.99. $$

We can check that this is satisfied when $R\geq 1/z^{2}$ .

Now, we can pick $F$ to be sufficiently small such that the second condition is satisfied. Lastly, we can pick $k$ to be sufficiently large so that the third condition is satisfied.

In particular, if we set $\gamma=1$ , we can pick the following values. We can set $R=500$ , so $m=$54\,108$$ . Then, we must take $F\leq\frac{$3.97\text{\times}{10}^{-15}$}{Lp}$ . If we set $k=12/F$ , then we have $(1-F)^{k}\leq e^{-12}\leq\frac{1}{2(m-1)}$ .

Thus, we have the following result:

#### Theorem 3.17 (Weak hardness for stable algorithms).

Take any constants $p>0$ , $L>0$ , $0<\gamma\leq 1$ and $f=o(n)$ . Then, for some sufficiently small $F$ and sufficiently large $k$ , there exists no $\left(f,L,\mathfrak{d},\Xi_{F},p_{\mathrm{st}}\right)$ -stable and $(\gamma,p_{\mathrm{f}})$ -optimal quantum algorithm for the Quantum Hypergraph Max-Cut problem for sufficiently small $p_{\mathrm{st}},p_{\mathrm{f}}\geq 0$ (depending only on $\gamma$ ) and $\mathfrak{d}\geq\max\left(\left\lceil e^{2}p\right\rceil,1\right)$ . In particular, when $\gamma=1$ , we can take $p_{\mathrm{st}}=p_{\mathrm{f}}=$1\text{\times}{10}^{-6}$$ , set $F=\frac{$3.97\text{\times}{10}^{-15}$}{Lp}$ and $k=$3.03\text{\times}{10}^{15}$Lp\geq 12/F$ .

#### Proof.

From Lemma 2.16, we know that $p_{\mathrm{b}}=e^{-\Omega(n)}$ . Since $m$ in the calculation above can be chosen to be sufficiently large depending only on $\gamma$ , we can take sufficiently small $p_{\mathrm{st}},p_{\mathrm{f}}\geq 0$ such that

$$ \displaystyle 1-3mp_{\mathrm{st}}-3mp_{\mathrm{f}}-mp_{\mathrm{b}}-me^{-3pFn(3\log 2-2)}\geq 0. $$

We can check that for $\gamma=1$ , this is satisfied when $p_{\mathrm{st}}=p_{\mathrm{f}}=$1\text{\times}{10}^{-6}$$ .

By Corollary 3.14, if we set $\epsilon=\log 2$ , we have that $2\log(1/\epsilon)<1$ , so if we have $\mathfrak{d}\geq\max\left(\left\lceil e^{2}p\right\rceil,1\right)$ , then we must have

$$ \Pr\left[\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}(\boldsymbol{S})\right]\geq 2^{-n}. $$

So, assuming that a stable and near-optimal algorithm as in the statement exists, by Lemma 3.12, with probability $(1+o_{n}(1))2^{-n}$ there exist bit strings $\mathbf{s}^{(t,r)}$ for $t\in[m]$ , $r\in[R]$ such that for all $t\neq t^{\prime}\in[m]$

$$ \frac{1}{Rn}\sum_{r=1}^{R}d_{\mathrm{H}}\left(\mathbf{s}^{(t,r)},\mathbf{s}^{(t^{\prime},r)}\right)\leq\frac{2\beta f}{n}+9\beta LpF, $$

and for all $t\in[m]$ , if $\gamma=1/2$ and $\delta=1/4$ , then

$$ \max_{r\in[R]}V\left(\boldsymbol{X}^{(t)},\mathbf{s}^{(t,r)}\right)\geq\frac{1}{3}\left(\gamma-\delta\right)E_{\ast}\geq\frac{1}{12}\sqrt{2p\log 2}, $$

but by the calculation above, this can only happen with probability less than $(1+o_{n}(1))2^{-n}$ . Thus, we have a contradiction and so no such algorithm can exist. ∎

## 4. Strong Hardness for Local Algorithms

In the previous section, we were able to show a statement roughly of the form “for any $L$ , there exists a $k$ such that all $L$ -stable algorithms fail”. However, ideally, we would like to make a stronger statement, of the form “there exists a fixed value of $k$ such that no stable algorithm is optimal”. Unfortunately, we are not able to show a sufficiently strong version of the Quantum Overlap Gap property for Quantum Hypergraph Max-Cut to establish a statement of this form. However, such a statement can be made if we strengthen our notion of stability and consider “local algorithms.” Instead of using the quantum Wasserstein distance of order $2$ ( $W_{2}$ ) as our distance metric, this notion of stability will use $W_{\infty}$ :

#### Definition 4.1 (Local algorithm).

Let $\Xi$ be a probability distribution over pairs $(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime})$ of problem instances that correspond to the same interaction hypergraph. Then, we say that a quantum algorithm $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}$ is $(f,L,\mathfrak{d},\Xi,p_{\mathrm{st}})$ -local if

$$ \Pr_{(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\sim\Xi\otimes\mathbb{P}_{\Omega}}\left[\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)-\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rVert_{W_{\infty}}\leq f+L\left\lVert\boldsymbol{X}-\boldsymbol{X}\right\rVert_{1}\mid\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}(\boldsymbol{X})\right]\geq 1-p_{\mathrm{st}}. $$

### 4.1. Local Algorithms Imply the Existence of Forbidden Configurations

#### 4.1.1. Reduction to Weakly Local Algorithms with Classical Outputs

The beginning of this proof proceeds similarly to Section 3. We do a reduction to deterministic algorithms and then algorithms with classical outputs that are “weakly local”. However, the properties of the $W_{\infty}$ distance allow us to derive much stronger results from the “weakly local” condition than from the “weakly stable” one.

#### Lemma 4.2.

Let $\left(\Xi^{(q)}\right)_{q\in[Q]}$ be a set of probability distributions of pairs of problem instances whose marginal distributions are all $\Lambda$ . Suppose that there exists a quantum algorithm $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)$ that is $\left(f,L,\mathfrak{d},\Xi^{(q)},p_{\mathrm{st}}\right)$ -local for all $q\in[Q]$ and $(\gamma,p_{\mathrm{f}})$ -optimal for $\Lambda$ . Then, there exists a deterministic quantum algorithm $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}(\boldsymbol{X})$ that is $\left(f,L,\mathfrak{d},\Xi,3Qp_{\mathrm{st}}\right)$ -local and $(\gamma,3p_{\mathrm{f}})$ -optimal for $\Lambda$ .

#### Proof.

The proof parallels that of Lemma 3.5, with an additional union bound. We have that

$$ \displaystyle\EE_{\omega\sim\mathbb{P}_{\Omega}}\left[\Pr_{(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime})\sim\Xi^{(q)}}\left[\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)-\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rVert_{W_{\infty}}>f+L\left\lVert\boldsymbol{X}-\boldsymbol{X}\right\rVert_{1}\mid\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}(\boldsymbol{X})\right]\right]= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\Pr_{(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\sim\Xi\otimes\mathbb{P}_{\Omega}}\left[\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)-\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rVert_{W_{2}}>f+L\left\lVert\boldsymbol{X}-\boldsymbol{X}\right\rVert_{1}\mid\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}(\boldsymbol{X})\right]\leq p_{\mathrm{st}}, $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\EE_{\omega\sim\mathbb{P}_{\Omega}}\left[\Pr_{\boldsymbol{X}\sim\Lambda}\left[\Tr\left(\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right)<\gamma E_{\ast}\right]\right]= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\Pr_{(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\sim\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{P}_{\Omega}}\left[\Tr\left(\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right)<\gamma E_{\ast}\right]\leq p_{\mathrm{f}}. $$

So, by Markov’s inequality, we have that

$$ \displaystyle\Pr_{\omega\sim\mathbb{P}_{\Omega}}\Bigg[\Pr_{(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime})\sim\Xi^{(q)}}\Big[\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)-\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rVert_{W_{2}}> \displaystyle>f+L\left\lVert\boldsymbol{X}-\boldsymbol{X}\right\rVert_{1}\mid\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}(\boldsymbol{X})\Big]>3Qp_{\mathrm{st}}\Bigg]\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\frac{1}{3Qp_{\mathrm{st}}}\EE_{\omega\sim\mathbb{P}_{\Omega}}\Bigg[\Pr_{(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime})\sim\Xi^{(q)}}\Big[\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)-\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rVert_{W_{\infty}}> \displaystyle>f+L\left\lVert\boldsymbol{X}-\boldsymbol{X}\right\rVert_{1}\mid\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}(\boldsymbol{X})\Big]\Bigg]\leq\frac{1}{3Q}, $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\Pr_{\omega\sim\mathbb{P}_{\Omega}}\left[\Pr_{\boldsymbol{X}\sim\Lambda}\left[\Tr\left(\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right)<\gamma E_{\ast}\right]>3p_{\mathrm{f}}\right]\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\frac{1}{3p_{\mathrm{f}}}\EE_{\omega\sim\mathbb{P}_{\Omega}}\left[\Pr_{\boldsymbol{X}\sim\Lambda}\left[\Tr\left(\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right)<\gamma E_{\ast}\right]\right]\leq\frac{1}{3}. $$

So now, by the union bound, we have that

$$ \displaystyle\Pr_{\omega\sim\mathbb{P}_{\Omega}}\Bigg[\Pr_{\boldsymbol{X}\sim\Lambda}\left[\Tr\left(\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right)<\gamma E_{\ast}\right]>3p_{\mathrm{f}}\vee \displaystyle\vee\bigvee_{q\in[Q]}\Pr_{(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime})\sim\Xi^{(q)}}\Big[\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)-\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rVert_{W_{\infty}}> \displaystyle>f+L\left\lVert\boldsymbol{X}-\boldsymbol{X}\right\rVert_{1}\mid\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}(\boldsymbol{X})\Big]>3p_{\mathrm{st}}\Bigg]\leq\frac{2}{3}. $$

Thus, there must exist some $\omega^{\ast}\in\Omega$ such that for all $q\in[Q]$ we have

$$ \displaystyle\Pr_{(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime})\sim\Xi^{(q)}}\left[\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega^{\ast})-\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega^{\ast})\right\rVert_{W_{\infty}}\leq f+L\left\lVert\boldsymbol{X}-\boldsymbol{X}\right\rVert_{1}\mid\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}(\boldsymbol{X})\right]\geq \displaystyle\geq{} \displaystyle 1-3Qp_{\mathrm{st}}, $$

and

$$ \Pr_{\boldsymbol{X}\sim\Lambda}\left[\Tr\left(\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega^{\ast})\right)\geq\gamma E_{\ast}\right]\geq 1-3p_{\mathrm{f}}. $$

Thus, if we define $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}(\boldsymbol{X})\coloneq\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega^{\ast})$ , then $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}$ is a deterministic quantum algorithm that is $\left(f,L,\Xi,3p_{\mathrm{st}}\right)$ -stable and $(\gamma,3p_{\mathrm{f}})$ -optimal. ∎

#### Lemma 4.3.

Let $\left(\Xi^{(q)}\right)_{q\in[Q]}$ be a probability distribution of pairs of problem instances whose marginal distributions are all $\Lambda$ . Suppose that the Pauli shadows estimator is $(\delta,p_{\mathrm{est}},p_{\mathrm{b}})$ -efficient for the class of Hamiltonians $\boldsymbol{H}(\Lambda)$ . Suppose there exists a deterministic quantum algorithm $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}$ that is $\left(f,L,\mathfrak{d},\Xi^{(q)},3Qp_{\mathrm{st}}\right)$ -local for all $q\in[Q]$ and $(\gamma,3p_{\mathrm{f}})$ -optimal for $\Lambda$ . Then, there exists a pure quantum algorithm $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}:\mathbb{R}^{\binom{n}{k}}\times[0,1]\rightarrow\{0,1\}^{n}$ (that is, a randomized algorithm outputting only classical states), such that the following weaker notion of locality holds for all $q\in[Q]$ :

$$ \displaystyle\Pr_{(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime})\sim\Xi}\Bigg[\left\lVert\EE_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right|-\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right|\right]\right\rVert_{W_{\infty}}\leq \displaystyle\leq f+L\left\lVert\boldsymbol{X}-\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{1}\mid\mathcal{X}_{\mathfrak{d}}(\boldsymbol{X})\Bigg]\geq 1-3Qp_{\mathrm{st}}. $$

Furthermore, consider some $\boldsymbol{X}$ that satisfies the following two conditions (which is true with probability at least $1-3p_{\mathrm{f}}-p_{\mathrm{b}}$ over $\boldsymbol{X}\sim\Lambda$ ):

$$ \Tr\left(\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}(\boldsymbol{X})\right)\geq\gamma E_{\ast} $$

$$ \Pr_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[\Tr\left(3\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{M}}}(\boldsymbol{\rho},\omega)\right)-\Tr\left(\boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{X})\boldsymbol{\rho}\right)\geq-\delta E_{\ast}\right]\geq 1-p_{\mathrm{est}}\quad\forall\boldsymbol{\rho}\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{m}}_{n}. $$

For such $\boldsymbol{X}$ , we must have that

$$ \Pr_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[V\left(\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right)\geq\frac{1}{3}(\gamma-\delta)E_{\ast}\right]\geq 1-p_{\mathrm{est}}. $$

#### Proof.

The proof is identical to that of Lemma 3.6. ∎

#### 4.1.2. Solution Configurations over Interpolation Paths

#### Proposition 4.4 (Stronger version of Proposition 3.7 for $W_{\infty}$ ).

For each problem instance $\boldsymbol{X}$ , let $p_{\boldsymbol{X}}(\mathbf{s})$ be the probability distribution of $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\in\{0,1\}^{n}$ over $\omega\sim\mathcal{U}$ . Then, for every pair of problem instances $\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime}$ , there exists a joint distribution $\pi_{\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime}}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\max_{(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{s}^{\prime})\in\supp\left(\pi_{\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime}}\right)}d_{\mathrm{H}}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{s}^{\prime})\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\left\lVert\EE_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right|-\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right|\right]\right\rVert_{W_{\infty}}. $$

#### Proof.

Write

$$ \boldsymbol{A}\coloneq\EE_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right|-\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right|\right]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\boldsymbol{A}_{i}, $$

where the $\boldsymbol{A}_{i}$ are Hermitian such that $\Tr_{\{i\}}\left(\boldsymbol{A}_{i}\right)=0$ , picked to be the optimal in Definition 2.7. That is, suppose (without loss of generality) that $\left\lVert\boldsymbol{A}_{i}\right\rVert_{\ast}\neq 0$ only for $i\leq W$ , where

$$ W=\left\lVert\EE_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right|-\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right|\right]\right\rVert_{W_{\infty}}. $$

Since, as in Proposition 3.7, we can write

$$ \left\lVert\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{A}_{i}\right\rVert_{\ast}=\Tr\left(\boldsymbol{A}_{i}^{+}\right)=\Tr\left(\boldsymbol{A}_{i}^{-}\right), $$

we must have that $\boldsymbol{A}_{i}=0$ for $i>W$ . Now, we can think of $\boldsymbol{A}$ as specifying a flow on a hypercube, with each $\boldsymbol{A}_{i}$ representing a flow along the $i$ ’th dimension, with the positive eigenvalues corresponding to sinks and negative eigenvalues to sources. Then, we can construct the joint distribution $\pi$ to describe the net flow from the sum of these contributions, and observe that $\pi(\boldsymbol{s},\boldsymbol{s}^{\prime})=0$ for any $\boldsymbol{s},\boldsymbol{s}^{\prime}$ with $\boldsymbol{s}_{i}\neq\boldsymbol{s}^{\prime}_{i}$ for any $i>W$ since there is no flow along dimension $i$ of the hypercube for $i>W$ . Thus,

$$ \displaystyle\max_{(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{s}^{\prime})\in\supp\left(\pi_{\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime}}\right)}d_{\mathrm{H}}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{s}^{\prime})\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle W=\left\lVert\EE_{\omega\sim\mathcal{U}}\left[\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X},\omega)\right|-\left|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right\rangle\left\langle\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{X}^{\prime},\omega)\right|\right]\right\rVert_{W_{\infty}}. $$

∎

#### Definition 4.5 (Distribution of problem instances for interpolation path).

For $T,Q\in\mathbb{N}$ , we define the distribution $\Xi_{Q,T}$ of collections $\left(\boldsymbol{X}^{(q,t)}\right)_{0\leq q\leq Q,t\in[T]}$ as follows. First, sample $\boldsymbol{S}$ by setting each $S_{A}\sim\Bern\left(p/\binom{n-1}{p-1}\right)$ i.i.d. Then, sample $\hat{\boldsymbol{J}},\widetilde{\boldsymbol{J}}^{(1)},\dots,\widetilde{\boldsymbol{J}}^{(T)}$ with i.i.d. entries in $\{-1,1\}$ . Then, for all and $A\in\binom{[n]}{k}$ , set

$$ X^{(q,t)}_{A}=\begin{cases}S_{A}\widetilde{J}^{(t)}_{A}&\text{ if }A\cap\left[\left\lceil qn/Q\right\rceil\right]\neq\varnothing\\
S_{A}\hat{J}_{A}&\text{ otherwise. }\end{cases} $$

In other words, we are interpolating between $\hat{\boldsymbol{X}}$ and $T$ other independent problem instances by resampling the weights of hyperedges intersecting with the first $q/Q$ fraction of qubits. In contrast to Definition 3.9, where we only considered a single interpolation step, here we are considering the whole path between two independent instances. We call the marginal distribution of $\left(\boldsymbol{X}^{(q-1,t)},\boldsymbol{X}^{(q,t)}\right)$ for a fixed $q,t$ by the name $\Xi_{Q}^{(q)}$ . Observe that these marginal distributions are independent of $t$ . We also have that the marginal distribution of $\left(\boldsymbol{X}^{(q,t)}\right)_{t\in[T]}$ for a fixed $q$ is the same as $\Xi_{\frac{q}{Q},T}$ as in Definition 3.9. Also, observe that when sampling from this distribution, we will always have $\boldsymbol{X}^{(0,t)}=\boldsymbol{X}^{(0,t^{\prime})}=\hat{\boldsymbol{X}}$ for all $t,t^{\prime}\in[T]$ .
