#### Theorem 3 (No spurious local minima, formal version of Theorem 2).

For some $p=O(\poly(L))$ , define:

$$ \tilde{\ell}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\coloneq\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})+\xi(\boldsymbol{\theta}) $$

where we have defined the perturbation:

$$ \xi\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}\right)\coloneq\epsilon\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left(a_{i}\cos(\theta_{i})+b_{i}\sin(\theta_{i})\right), $$

where $\epsilon>0$ , $\boldsymbol{\theta}\in[0,2\pi)^{p}$ , and $a_{i},b_{i}$ are i.i.d. standard Gaussian (independent from the coefficients in the QNN ansatz). the expected number of critical points $\tilde{\ell}$ above the global minimum approaches $0$ as $\epsilon\to 0^{+}$ .

#### Proof.

We choose $p$ sufficiently large as in Proposition 2 so that the Hessian becomes singular. Now, consider the perturbation term $\xi:[0,2\pi)^{p}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ as defined in the theorem statement. Observe that $\xi$ is a smooth function on the $p$ -torus and its distribution is rotationally invariant. Furthermore, the second derivative of $\xi$ with respect to any $\theta_{i}$ is nonzero with high probability, and the marginal probability density of the gradient of $\xi$ at any $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ is continuous. If we consider $\tilde{\ell}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})+\xi(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ , we can now check the following conditions for applying the Kac-Rice formula (Adler and Taylor, 2007), as stated in Anschuetz (2022).

- (1) All components of $\tilde{\ell},\nabla\tilde{\ell},\nabla^{2}\tilde{\ell}$ are almost surely continuous and have finite variances over $[0,2\pi)^{p}$ .

- (2) At any $\boldsymbol{\theta}\in[0,2\pi)^{p}$ , the marginal probability density $\mathfrak{p}\left(\nabla\tilde{\ell}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\right)$ is continuous at $\nabla\tilde{\ell}(\boldsymbol{\theta)}=0$ .

- (3) The conditional density of $\nabla\tilde{\ell}(\boldsymbol{\theta)}$ conditioned on $\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta}),\nabla^{2}\tilde{\ell}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ is bounded above and continuous at $\nabla\tilde{\ell}(\boldsymbol{\theta)}=0$ , uniformly in $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ .

- (4) The conditional density of $\det\left(\nabla^{2}\tilde{\ell}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\right)$ conditioned on $\nabla\tilde{\ell}(\boldsymbol{\theta)}=0$ is continuous at $\det\left(\nabla^{2}\tilde{\ell}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\right)=0$ , uniformly in $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ .

- (5) The conditional density of $\tilde{\ell}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ conditioned on $\nabla\tilde{\ell}(\boldsymbol{\theta)}=0$ is continuous for values of $\tilde{\ell}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ and $\nabla\tilde{\ell}(\boldsymbol{\theta)}$ in a neighborhood of $0$ , uniformly in $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ .

- (6) The $p$ th moments of the entries of the Hessian are bounded, uniformly in $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ .

- (7) The moduli of continuity $\omega$ of the components of $\tilde{\ell}(\boldsymbol{\theta}),\nabla\tilde{\ell}(\boldsymbol{\theta)},\nabla^{2}\tilde{\ell}(\boldsymbol{\theta)}$ satisfy $\Pr\left[\omega(\eta)>\delta\right]=o(\eta^{p})$ for all $\delta>0$ as $\eta\rightarrow 0^{+}$ .

Anschuetz (2022) demonstrated that these assumptions hold for variational loss landscapes; for us, the main difference is ensuring conditions (4) and (5), since we are looking at the overparameterized regime where the original Hessian is singular.

(1) follows by the construction of the QNN ansatz, (2) and (3) can be seen by considering the approximation to the distribution of the gradient in Theorem 1. (4) is ensured by adding the perturbation term $\xi(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ to the loss, which makes the Hessian non-singular with high probability. Similarly, for condition (5), the perturbation term breaks any symmetry in critical manifolds with high probability, thus making the conditional density of $\tilde{\ell}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ continuous. (6) holds since the second derivatives are uniformly bounded. (7) holds by the argument in Anschuetz (2022).

We can now apply the Kac-Rice formula, which says that the expected number of local minima with loss values greater than the optimum $\ell_{\ast}$ is given by

$$ \int_{[0,2\pi)^{p}}\mathfrak{p}\left(\nabla\tilde{\ell}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=0\right)\EE\left[\left\lvert\det\left(\nabla^{2}\tilde{\ell}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\right)\right\rvert\mathbbm{1}\left[\tilde{\ell}(\boldsymbol{\theta})>\ell_{\ast}\wedge\nabla^{2}\tilde{\ell}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\succeq 0\right]\mid\nabla\tilde{\ell}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=0\right]\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}. $$

Since $\epsilon$ can be made arbitrarily small and the determinant is a continuous function of the entries of the Hessian, the expectation of the determinant in the integrand above can also be made arbitrarily small. Since the density of the gradient at zero is bounded, and the gradient is not affected by the perturbation to leading order in $\epsilon$ , the probability density term in the integrand remains bounded. Thus, the statement follows. ∎

## Appendix B Details on the Lévy-Prokhorov Metric and Error Bounds

#### Definition 2 (Lévy-Prokhorov Metric).

Consider two probability measures $F$ , $G$ over $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , we define the Lévy-Prokhorov distance between $F$ and $G$ relative to a norm $\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert$ on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ as

$$ \pi(F,G)=\inf\{\epsilon>0:F(A)<G(A^{\epsilon})+\epsilon\;\forall\;A\}, $$

where $A$ ranges over the Borel sets in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $A^{\epsilon}$ is an $\epsilon$ -neighborhood of $A$ in the given norm.

#### Lemma 6.

$\pi(F,G)=\pi(G,F)$ .

#### Proof.

Suppose that for all Borel sets $A$ , we have $F(A)<G(A^{\epsilon})+\epsilon$ . Then,

$$ F(A^{c})<G((A^{c})^{\epsilon})+\epsilon. $$

For $\epsilon>0$ , define $A^{-\epsilon}$ to be the set of all points $x$ such that the open $\epsilon$ -ball centered at $x$ is contained in $A$ . Then, observe that

$$ \overline{(A^{c})^{\epsilon}}=\overline{(A^{-\epsilon})^{c}}, $$

which means that we can write

$$ \displaystyle 1-F(A) \displaystyle<1-G(A^{-\epsilon})+\epsilon \displaystyle G(A^{-\epsilon}) \displaystyle<F(A)+\epsilon $$

Now, since for all $A$ , we have $A\subseteq(A^{\epsilon})^{-\epsilon}$ , so we can substitute

$$ G(A)\leq G((A^{\epsilon})^{-\epsilon})<F(A^{\epsilon})+\epsilon. $$

Thus, $\pi(F,G)=\pi(G,F)$ . ∎

#### Definition 3 (Convolution).

If $\varphi,\gamma$ are the probability densities of the distributions $F,G$ , then the probability density of the convolution $F\ast G$ is defined to be

$$ \rho(t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\varphi(x)\gamma(t-x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x. $$

#### Definition 4 (Characteristic Function).

The characteristic function of a distribution $F$ with density $\varphi$ is defined as

$$ f(t)=\EE[e^{\boldsymbol{\mathrm{i}}tX}]=\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{\boldsymbol{\mathrm{i}}tx}\varphi(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x, $$

where in the above $X\sim F$ is a random variable.

#### Lemma 7.

Let $F$ , $G$ , and $H$ be probability distributions on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , and let $r>0$ . Then, the following inequality holds:

$$ \pi(F,G)\leq\pi(F\ast H,G\ast H)+2\max\{r,H(\left\lVert x\right\rVert\geq r)\}, $$

#### Proof.

Let $X\sim F$ , $Y\sim H$ be independent random variables. Let $A,K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}$ . We know that

$$ \displaystyle(F\ast H)(A)=\Pr[X+Y\in A]\geq \displaystyle\geq{} \displaystyle\Pr[X+k\in A\;\forall k\in K]\Pr[Y\in K]\geq \displaystyle\geq{} \displaystyle\Pr[X+k\in A\;\forall k\in K]+\Pr[Y\in K]-1= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle F(\{x:x+K\subseteq A\})+H(K)-1. $$

Thus, letting $K$ be the open ball of radius $\epsilon$ , we have that

$$ (F\ast H)(A^{\epsilon})\geq F(A)+H(\left\lVert x\right\rVert<\epsilon)-1=F(A)-H(\left\lVert x\right\rVert\geq\epsilon). $$

Note that we use the shorthand notation $H(\left\lVert x\right\rVert<\epsilon)$ to mean $H(\{x:\left\lVert x\right\rVert<\epsilon)\}$ .

Now, we can also argue that

$$ \displaystyle(F\ast H)(A)=\Pr[X+Y\in A]\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\Pr[X\in A-K]\Pr[Y\in K]+\Pr[Y\in K^{c}]\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\Pr[X\in A-K]+\Pr[Y\in K^{c}]=F(A-K)+H(K^{c}). $$

This gives us the inequality

$$ (F\ast H)(A)\leq F(A^{\epsilon})+H(\left\lVert x\right\rVert\geq\epsilon). $$

The same holds when replacing $F$ with $G$ . Now, if we let $L=\pi(F\ast H,G\ast H)$ , then we must have by the above and by the definition of the Lévy-Prokhorov metric that

$$ \displaystyle F(A)\leq(F\ast H)(A^{r})+H(\left\lVert x\right\rVert\geq r)\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle(G\ast H)(A^{r+L})+H(\left\lVert x\right\rVert\geq r)+L\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle G(A^{2r+L})+2H(\left\lVert x\right\rVert\geq r)+L\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle G(A^{L+2\max\{r,H(\left\lVert x\right\rVert\geq r)\}})+2H(\left\lVert x\right\rVert\geq r)+L+2\max\{r,H(\left\lVert x\right\rVert\geq r)\}, $$

which proves that

$$ \pi(F,G)\leq\pi(F\ast H,G\ast H)+2\max\{r,H(\left\lVert x\right\rVert\geq r)\}. $$

∎

#### Lemma 8.

(This lemma is adapted from Lemma 2.2 of Berkes and Philipp (1979)). Let $F$ and $G$ be probability distributions on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with characteristic functions $f$ and $g$ , respectively. Then, for some sufficiently large $T=O(d)$ , we have that the Lévy-Prokhorov metric relative to the Euclidean norm is bounded as

$$ \pi_{2}(F,G)<\left(\frac{T}{\pi}\right)^{d}\int_{\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{2}\leq T}\left\lvert f(u)-g(u)\right\rvert\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u+F(\{x:\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{2}\geq T/2\})+16d\frac{\log T}{T}. $$

Let $H$ be a distribution on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with density $\nu(x)$ and characteristic function $h\in L^{1}$ . Let $F_{1}=F\ast H$ and $G_{1}=G\ast H$ . Let $\varphi$ and $\gamma$ be the probability densities of $F_{1}$ and $G_{1}$ , respectively. Their characteristic functions are $f_{1}=fh$ and $g_{1}=gh$ . Now, using the definition of convolution and applying the inverse Fourier transform, we have

$$ \displaystyle\left\lvert\varphi(x)-\gamma(x)\right\rvert=(2\pi)^{-d}\left\lvert\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{-\boldsymbol{\mathrm{i}}\langle u,x\rangle}(f_{1}(u)-g_{1}(u))\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u\right\rvert\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left\lvert(f(u)-g(u))\right\rvert\left\lvert h(u)\right\rvert\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle(2\pi)^{-d}\left(\int_{\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{2}\leq T}\left\lvert(f(u)-g(u))\right\rvert\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u+2\int_{\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{2}\geq T}\left\lvert h(u)\right\rvert\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u\right), $$

where $T$ is any real number. Then, for any Borel set $B\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle F_{1}(B)-G_{1}(B)\leq F_{1}(B\cap\{\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{2}\leq T\})-G_{1}(B\cap\{\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{2}\leq T\})+F_{1}(\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{2}\geq T)\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\int_{\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{2}\leq T}\left\lvert\varphi(x)-\gamma(x)\right\rvert\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x+F(\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{2}\geq T/2)+H(\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{2}\geq T/2)\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\left(\frac{T}{\pi}\right)^{d}\left(\int_{\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{2}\leq T}\left\lvert(f(u)-g(u))\right\rvert\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u+2\int_{\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{2}\geq T}\left\lvert h(u)\right\rvert\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u\right)+ \displaystyle+F(\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{2}\geq T/2)+H(\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{2}\geq T/2). $$

Since for all $B$

$$ F_{1}(B)=G_{1}(B)+(F_{1}(B)-G_{1}(B))\leq G_{1}(B^{(F_{1}(B)-G_{1}(B))})+(F_{1}(B)-G_{1}(B)), $$

we have that

$$ \pi(F_{1},G_{1})\leq\left\lvert F_{1}(B)-G_{1}(B)\right\rvert. $$

We also know from Lemma 7 that for any $r>0$ ,

$$ \pi(F,G)\leq\pi(F_{1},G_{1})+2\max\{r,H(\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{2}\geq r)\}. $$

Now, if we choose $r\leq T/2$ , we can put this together to get

$$ \displaystyle\pi(F,G)\leq\left(\frac{T}{\pi}\right)^{d}\left(\int_{\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{2}\leq T}\left\lvert(f(u)-g(u))\right\rvert\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u+2\int_{\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{2}\geq T}\left\lvert h(u)\right\rvert\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u\right)+ \displaystyle+F(\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{2}\geq T/2)+3\max\{r,H(\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{2}\geq r)\}. $$

Now, let $\sigma=3d^{1/2}T^{-1}\log^{1/2}T$ and $r=5dT^{-1}\log T$ . Let $H$ be a distribution with probability density

$$ \nu(x)=(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{-d/2}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}\sum_{j=1}^{d}x_{j}^{2}\right). $$

Then,

$$ \displaystyle h(u)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{\boldsymbol{\mathrm{i}}\langle u,x\rangle}\nu(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{-d/2}\prod_{j=1}^{d}\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{\boldsymbol{\mathrm{i}}u_{j}x-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}x^{2}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{-d/2}\prod_{j=1}^{d}\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}(x^{2}-2\boldsymbol{\mathrm{i}}\sigma^{2}u_{j}x-\sigma^{4}u_{j}^{2}+\sigma^{4}u_{j}^{2})}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{-d/2}\prod_{j=1}^{d}\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}(x-\boldsymbol{\mathrm{i}}\sigma^{2}u_{j})^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}u_{j}^{2}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{-d/2}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}\sum_{j=1}^{d}u_{j}^{2}\right)\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}x^{2}}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\right)^{d}= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}\sum_{j=1}^{d}u_{j}^{2}\right). $$

Note that we are able to remove the $\boldsymbol{\mathrm{i}}\sigma^{2}u_{j}$ term in the exponent in the integrand, because the integrand is an entire function and so its integral around a rectangle with one side on the real axis and one side shifted by $-\boldsymbol{\mathrm{i}}\sigma^{2}u_{j}$ must be zero. Since the the contribution of the other two sides of the rectangle goes to zero, the value of the integral remains the same when moved to the real axis.

So now, we have that

$$ \displaystyle\pi(F,G)\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\left(\frac{T}{\pi}\right)^{d}\left(\int_{\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{2}\leq T}\left\lvert(f(u)-g(u))\right\rvert\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u+2\int_{\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{2}\geq T}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}\sum_{j=1}^{d}u_{j}^{2}\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u\right)+ \displaystyle+F(\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{2}\geq T/2)+3\max\left\{r,(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{-d/2}\int_{\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{2}\geq r}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}\sum_{j=1}^{d}u_{j}^{2}\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u\right\}. $$

Now, observe that for any $A$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{2}\geq A}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{d}u_{j}^{2}\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u=(2\pi)^{d/2}\Pr[\chi_{d}^{2}\geq A^{2}]=(2\pi)^{d/2}\Pr\left[e^{\frac{3}{8}\chi_{d}^{2}}\geq e^{\frac{3}{8}A^{2}}\right]\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle(2\pi)^{d/2}e^{-3A^{2}/8}\EE\left[e^{\frac{3}{8}\chi_{d}^{2}}\right]=(2\pi)^{d/2}e^{-3A^{2}/8}2^{d}. $$

Going back to our previous expression, we can substitute $v_{j}=\sigma u_{j}$ for the second integral and $v_{j}=u_{j}/\sigma$ for the third, which gives us

$$ \displaystyle\pi(F,G)\leq\left(\frac{T}{\pi}\right)^{d}\left(\int_{\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{2}\leq T}\left\lvert(f(u)-g(u))\right\rvert\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u+\frac{2}{\sigma^{d}}\int_{\left\lvert v\right\rvert\geq\sigma T}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{d}v_{j}^{2}\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}v\right)+ \displaystyle+F(\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{2}\geq T/2)+3\max\left\{r,(2\pi)^{-d/2}\int_{\left\lvert v\right\rvert\geq r/\sigma}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{d}v_{j}^{2}\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}v\right\}= \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\left(\frac{T}{\pi}\right)^{d}\left(\int_{\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{2}\leq T}\left\lvert(f(u)-g(u))\right\rvert\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u+\frac{2}{\sigma^{d}}(2\pi)^{d/2}e^{-3T^{2}\sigma^{2}/8}2^{d}\right)+ \displaystyle+F(\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{2}\geq T/2)+3\max\left\{r,e^{-\frac{3r^{2}}{8\sigma^{2}}}2^{d}\right\}. $$

Now, since

$$ \frac{3r^{2}}{8\sigma^{2}}=\frac{3}{8}\frac{25d^{2}T^{-2}\log^{2}T}{9dT^{-2}\log T}=\frac{25d\log T}{24}, $$

so the second term in the maximum becomes

$$ T^{-\frac{25d}{24}2^{d}} $$

which becomes subleading to

$$ r=\frac{5d\log T}{T} $$

for large $d$ . Also, we have that

$$ \frac{2}{\sigma^{d}}(2\pi)^{d/2}e^{-3T^{2}\sigma^{2}/8}2^{d}=\frac{2^{d+1}(2\pi)^{d/2}}{\left(3d^{1/2}T^{-1}\log^{1/2}T\right)^{d}}T^{-\frac{27}{8}d}, $$

which becomes subleading if $T$ is sufficiently large. Increasing the coefficient for $r$ by one to strictly dominate the subleading terms, we arrive at the final expression:

$$ \pi(F,G)\leq\left(\frac{T}{\pi}\right)^{d}\int_{\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{2}\leq T}\left\lvert(f(u)-g(u))\right\rvert\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u+F(\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{2}\geq T/2)+\frac{16d\log T}{T}. $$

∎

#### Corollary 1.

Let $F$ and $G$ be two distributions on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with density functions $\varphi$ and $\gamma$ and characteristic functions $f$ and $g$ respectively. Assume that there exists some $C$ such that

$$ \int_{\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{\infty}\geq C}f(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\leq\mu. $$

Then, there exists a universal constant $K$ such that for all $T\geq\max(2C\sqrt{d},Kd)$ , we have that

$$ \pi(F,G)\leq\left(\frac{T}{\pi}\right)^{d}\int_{\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq T}\left\lvert(f(u)-g(u))\right\rvert\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u+\frac{16d\log T}{T}+\mu. $$

#### Proof.

We need to convert from the Euclidean norm used in Lemma 8 to the infinity norm. We know that $\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{d}\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{\infty}$ , so after performing that change, the claim immediately follows. ∎

#### Lemma 9.

(This has been adapted from Corollary 38 of Anschuetz (2025)). Let $F,G$ be distributions on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with densities $\varphi,\gamma$ and characteristic functions $f,g$ . Assume that each moment of order $k^{\prime}\leq k$ of $F$ differs from that of $G$ by an additive error of at most $\epsilon>0$ and assume that all moments of order $k^{\prime}>k$ are bounded by $(C\sqrt{k^{\prime}})^{k^{\prime}}$ for some constant $C$ . Let $\zeta>0$ be a sufficiently small constant. Assume that

$$ \int_{\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{\infty}\geq\frac{1}{2\sqrt{d}}\min\left\{\frac{1-\zeta}{d}\log(\epsilon^{-1}),\frac{\sqrt{k+1}}{2eCd}\right\}}f(x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\leq\mu. $$

Also assume that

$$ d^{2}=o\left(\min\left\{\frac{\log(\epsilon^{-1})}{\log\log(\epsilon^{-1})},\frac{\sqrt{k}}{\log k}\right\}\right). $$

Then, the Lévy-Prokhorov distance is bounded by

$$ \pi(F,G)=O\left(\frac{d^{2}\log\log(\epsilon^{-1})}{\log(\epsilon^{-1})}+\frac{d^{2}\log k}{\sqrt{k}}+\mu\right). $$

#### Proof.

Let

$$ T=\min\left\{\frac{1-\zeta}{d}\log(\epsilon^{-1}),\frac{\sqrt{k+1}}{2eCd}\right\}. $$

This, with the stated assumptions, satisfies the conditions for applying Corollary 1, which gives us that

$$ \pi(F,G)\leq\widetilde{O}(T^{2d})\sup_{\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq T}\left\lvert f(u)-g(u)\right\rvert+O\left(\frac{d\log T}{T}\right)+O(\mu). $$

Since

$$ dT\leq\frac{\sqrt{k+1}}{2eC}, $$

we can apply Lemma 37 of Anschuetz (2025) to say that

$$ \sup_{\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq T}\left\lvert f(u)-g(u)\right\rvert\leq\sup_{\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{1}\leq dT}\left\lvert f(u)-g(u)\right\rvert\leq\epsilon e^{dT}+2^{1-k}\leq\epsilon^{\zeta}+2^{1-k}. $$

We also have that

$$ T^{2d}=\exp(2d\log T)=\exp\left(o(\min\{\log(\epsilon^{-1}),\sqrt{k}\})\right). $$

So,

$$ \widetilde{O}(T^{2d})\sup_{\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq T}\left\lvert f(u)-g(u)\right\rvert+O\left(\frac{d\log T}{T}\right)\leq O\left(\epsilon^{\zeta+\sqrt{k}}+e^{\sqrt{k}+(1-k)\log 2}\right). $$

Now, looking at the second term, we have that

$$ \displaystyle O\left(\frac{d\log T}{T}\right)\leq O\left(d\min\left\{\log\log(\epsilon^{-1}),\log k\right\}\max\left\{\frac{d}{\log(\epsilon^{-1})},\frac{d}{\sqrt{k}}\right\}\right)\leq \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle O\left(\frac{d^{2}\log\log(\epsilon^{-1})}{\log(\epsilon^{-1})}+\frac{d^{2}\log k}{\sqrt{k}}\right). $$

This second term dominates the first, which means that

$$ \pi(F,G)=O\left(\frac{d^{2}\log\log(\epsilon^{-1})}{\log(\epsilon^{-1})}+\frac{d^{2}\log k}{\sqrt{k}}+\mu\right). $$

∎

## Appendix C Numerical Experiments

In this appendix, we provide small-scale numerical experiments to illustrate our main results. We train our QNN model to perform fragment classification on the Temperley-Lieb model, using simple toy datasets. It is important to note that these experiments are not intended to serve as a demonstration of a direct practical application of our work, as the model we consider already admits efficient classical simulation techniques. They are also not meant to demonstrate any specific asymptotic scaling behavior proven in our main results, as simulating the QNN model classically becomes impractical for larger system sizes. The experiments serve as illustrative examples to demonstrate QNN trainability for the fragment classification task.

### C.1 QNN Training

*Figure 2: Training curves for QNN models with $1$ , $5$ , $10$ , and $15$ parameters on the $4$ -qubit Temperley-Lieb dataset. For each number of parameters, $10$ QNNs were randomly initialized and trained for $200$ epochs with a learning rate of $0.1$ . Training was stopped if the loss was decaying slower than $5\%$ every $5$ epochs or if it reached less than $0.01$ . The faded lines show the individual training curves, and the solid lines show their averages. For these diagrams, the loss value is adjusted to scale from $0$ to $1$ instead of from $-1$ to $0$ .*

*Figure 3: Training curves for QNN models with $10$ , $50$ , and $100$ parameters on the $6$ -qubit Temperley-Lieb dataset. For each number of parameters, a QNN was randomly initialized and trained for $200$ epochs with a learning rate of $1$ . Training was stopped if the loss was decaying slower than $5\%$ every $5$ epochs or if it reached less than $0.01$ . Note that the increase in the number of parameters needed compared to Figure 2 is due not just to the larger system size, but also to the increased number of dataset entries, doubling the dimension $N_{a}$ .*

We consider a Schur basis for the Temperley-Lieb model on $2$ -level quantum systems constructed in correspondence with the “dots and dimers” picture of Moudgalya and Motrunich (2022). For simplicity, we take a subset of such a basis consisting of states that can be expressed as tensor products of computational basis states and the EPR state $\left|\Phi^{+}\right\rangle$ . We demonstrate that our QNN model can be trained to distinguish states of this form with different configurations of entangled pairs, while generalizing across any valid state on the non-entangled qubits. We consider the following $2$ -entry dataset on a $4$ -qubit system:

$$ \mathcal{D}_{4}=\left\{\left|\Phi^{+}\right\rangle\otimes\left|01\right\rangle,\left|\Phi^{+}\right\rangle^{\otimes 2}\right\}, $$

and the following $4$ -entry dataset on a $6$ -qubit system:

$$ \mathcal{D}_{6}=\left\{\left|\Phi^{+}\right\rangle\otimes\left|0101\right\rangle,\left|0101\right\rangle\otimes\left|\Phi^{+}\right\rangle,\left|\Phi^{+}\right\rangle^{\otimes 2}\otimes\left|01\right\rangle,\left|\Phi^{+}\right\rangle^{\otimes 3}\right\}. $$

We then construct the QNN ansatz using local generators of the form $\left|\Phi^{+}\right\rangle\left\langle\Phi^{+}\right|_{(i,i+1)}$ , randomly selecting the Hamiltonian, the coefficients $t_{1},\dots,t_{p},t^{\prime},t^{\prime\prime}$ as in Section 3.1. The QNN is initialized with random parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ and optimized by gradient descent.

*Figure 4: Distribution of local minima reached during training for the $4$ -qubit Temperley-Lieb dataset. For this plot, $1000$ QNNs were randomly initialized for each number of parameters and trained for $200$ epochs with a learning rate of $0.1$ . The data plotted on the $x$ -axis is the final loss achieved during training. Since we can assume that during gradient descent the parameters converge to the “closest” local minimum, this is a proxy for the distribution of the local minima of the loss landscape. We can see that with $15$ parameters, the QNN enters the overparameterized regime since the distribution of minima becomes peaked at zero.*

The simulations were performed using the qutip library in Python. Since our simulations explicitly compute matrix products and exponentials of operators acting on the exponential-size Hilbert space, these methods become impractical for larger system sizes. That said, even at small system sizes our results—reported in Figures 2, 3 and 4—support the correctness of the QNN construction and illustrate the phenomenon of the overparameterized regime: there exists a number of parameters for which the QNN will almost always reach the global optimum loss during training.

### C.2 Empirical Tests of the ETH Assumption

Here we do a simple demonstration to support the claim that we can reasonably expect our Hamiltonians to satisfy the full ETH in each Krylov subspace for our analysis. For the Temperley-Lieb Hamiltonian considered in the QNN training experiments above, we numerically check that

$$ \mathbb{E}[\Tr(e^{-iHt}\left|x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|e^{iHt}O_{x})^{2}]-\mathbb{E}[\Tr(e^{-iHt}\left|x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|e^{iHt}O_{x})]^{2}=O(1/N^{*}_{\lambda}), $$

analogously to Equation (C3) of Fava et al. (2025), which we use in our Lemma 2. Here, $\left|x\right\rangle$ is a state from some subspace labelled by $\lambda$ —in this case, we take a state of the form $\left|\Phi^{+}\right\rangle\otimes\left|0101\dots\right\rangle$ , which is in a Krylov subspace whose dimension grows with system size. Note that for the purposes of our analysis, it is sufficient that quantities of this form decay with the system size (not necessarily as $O(1/N^{*}_{\lambda})$ ).
